genres.name: Mvamo
genres.start_label: Featured as audio example (track 25) on the Garland Handbook CD; documented in context of southern Malawian women's dance in Presbyterian churches.
genres.note: Mvamo is a traditional Malawian music and dance form documented across several ethnic communities without specific concentration in one geographic region.

sources.citation: Ruth M. Stone (ed.), The Garland Handbook of African Music, 2nd ed., Routledge, 2008, p. 442.

genres.name: Kyo
genres.start_label: Garland (1998) documents kyo as a living Burmese classical vocal genre; audio example recorded. No origin date assigned.
genres.note: Kyo is a traditional Burmese classical singing genre centered in Mandalay, the cultural capital of upper Burma and custodian of royal court traditions.

sources.citation: Terry E. Miller and Sean Williams, eds., The Garland Encyclopedia of World Music, vol. 4: Southeast Asia, Garland Publishing, 1998.

genres.name: Thachin
genres.start_label: Thachin is documented as the primary indigenous song form of Myanmar, pre-dating colonial period and continuing through present day.
genres.note: Thachin songs are the foundational classical Burmese vocal tradition maintained from the Konbaung era, forming the national court musical canon.

genres.name: Myanmar rock (1980s)
genres.start_label: Myanmar rock emerged in the 1980s with artists such as Iron Cross (Lay Phyu), influenced by Western rock but performed in Burmese; subject to SLORC censorship from 1988 through app
genres.note: Myanmar rock emerged in Yangon in the 1980s, blending electric guitar styles with Burmese rhythms in the commercial music venues of the southern capital.

genres.name: Myanmar hip-hop (1990s)
genres.start_label: Myanmar hip-hop emerged in the 1990s under SLORC/SPDC censorship; artists include G Fatt and Sai Sai Kham Leng. The scene grew rapidly after 2012 with improved internet access.
genres.note: Myanmar hip-hop developed in urban music scenes from the 1990s. Performers adapted rap and hip-hop forms within the country's changing popular-music culture.

genres.name: Mohori
genres.start_label: Garland (1998) documents mohori as a living folk theater genre with associated ensemble instrument set (kroeung mohori); no exact origin date given.
genres.note: Mohori is a Cambodian entertainment ensemble and repertory connected with sung performance and folk theater. Modernized mohori songs also entered Khmer popular music.

sources.citation: Terry E. Miller and Sean Williams, eds., The Garland Encyclopedia of World Music, vol. 4: Southeast Asia, Garland Publishing, 1998.

genres.name: Phleng Kar
genres.start_label: Garland (1998) describes the vungphleng kar as 'the most popular of all Khmer music ensembles'; no origin date assigned.
genres.note: Phleng kar is Cambodian wedding music played by a village ensemble. Its distinctive instruments and rhythms mark it apart from court and other ceremonial repertories.

sources.citation: Terry E. Miller and Sean Williams, eds., The Garland Encyclopedia of World Music, vol. 4: Southeast Asia, Garland Publishing, 1998.

genres.name: Yike
genres.start_label: Garland (1998) documents yike as a living genre; identifies Islamic influence as formative; no origin date assigned.
genres.note: Yike is a Khmer folk-theater form shaped partly by Islamic influences. Its song and instrumental performance became part of Cambodia's living theatrical repertory.

sources.citation: Terry E. Miller and Sean Williams, eds., The Garland Encyclopedia of World Music, vol. 4: Southeast Asia, Garland Publishing, 1998.

genres.name: Ramvong
genres.start_label: Ramvong is documented as a traditional Cambodian circle dance and music form central to folk identity. Disrupted by Khmer Rouge 1975–1979; subsequently reconstructed and revived.
genres.note: Ramvong is a Cambodian round dance in which women and men move together in a circle, using measured steps and graceful hand gestures. Related versions occur across Southeast Asia.

genres.name: Badawī
genres.start_label: Entry describes badawī as an Arab folk genre; Lebanese performers are documented in the modern popular form.
genres.note: Badawī is Arab Bedouin song shaped by oral poetry and storytelling, often dealing with love, generosity, and courage. Lebanese singers such as Samīra Tawfīq brought it to wider audiences.

sources.citation: Richard C. Jankowsky, vol. ed., Bloomsbury Encyclopedia of Popular Music of the World, vol. X: Genres: Middle East and North Africa, Bloomsbury Academic, 2015.

genres.name: Mawwāl
genres.start_label: Entry documents mawwāl as a leading Arab improvisatory vocal form with Lebanese performers among its leading figures.
genres.note: Mawwāl is a free-rhythm Arab vocal improvisation in which a solo singer stretches poetic syllables and explores a melodic mode. Lebanese singer Wadīʿ al-Ṣāfī made it a signature repertory.

sources.citation: Richard C. Jankowsky, vol. ed., Bloomsbury Encyclopedia of Popular Music of the World, vol. X: Genres: Middle East and North Africa, Bloomsbury Academic, 2015.

genres.name: Ṭarab
genres.start_label: Entry describes ṭarab as an eastern Arab world style peaking in the second half of the twentieth century.
genres.note: Ṭarab describes emotionally absorbing Arab art-music performance, often built through expressive singing, poetic text, and melodic improvisation. Lebanese singers Fayrūz and Ṣabāḥ worked in its mid-twentieth-century era.

sources.citation: Richard C. Jankowsky, vol. ed., Bloomsbury Encyclopedia of Popular Music of the World, vol. X: Genres: Middle East and North Africa, Bloomsbury Academic, 2015.

genres.name: Bashraf
genres.start_label: Entry traces bashraf to Ottoman court music and documents its practice across Levantine Arab cities.
genres.note: Bashraf is an instrumental form inherited from Ottoman court music and played within Arab classical suites. Beirut's Levantine music tradition shares the form with other eastern Arab cities.

sources.citation: Richard C. Jankowsky, vol. ed., Bloomsbury Encyclopedia of Popular Music of the World, vol. X: Genres: Middle East and North Africa, Bloomsbury Academic, 2015.

genres.name: Samāʿī
genres.start_label: Entry traces samāʿī to Ottoman court music and documents its practice across Levantine Arab cities.
genres.note: Samāʿī is an Ottoman-derived instrumental composition used in Arab classical suites. Its sections alternate with a recurring refrain, commonly over a distinctive ten-beat rhythm.

sources.citation: Richard C. Jankowsky, vol. ed., Bloomsbury Encyclopedia of Popular Music of the World, vol. X: Genres: Middle East and North Africa, Bloomsbury Academic, 2015.

genres.name: Ṭaqṭūqa
genres.start_label: Entry places the genre's peak popularity from the late nineteenth century through the mid-twentieth century; Lebanese examples are documented.
genres.note: Ṭaqṭūqa is a short Arab vocal form with a refrain returning between verses. Lebanese examples were recorded by Wadīʿ al-Ṣāfī and the Raḥbānī Brothers.

sources.citation: Richard C. Jankowsky, vol. ed., Bloomsbury Encyclopedia of Popular Music of the World, vol. X: Genres: Middle East and North Africa, Bloomsbury Academic, 2015.

genres.name: Ughniyya (Eastern Arab)
genres.start_label: Entry dates the new genre taxonomy to the early 1970s Lebanese TV show Studio al-Fann.
genres.note: Ughniyya is the modern Arab short-song category that displaced many older vocal forms in popular usage. A Lebanese television talent show helped establish its newer genre vocabulary in the 1970s.

sources.citation: Richard C. Jankowsky, vol. ed., Bloomsbury Encyclopedia of Popular Music of the World, vol. X: Genres: Middle East and North Africa, Bloomsbury Academic, 2015.

genres.name: Umhlanga Reed Dance music
genres.start_label: The Umhlanga Reed Dance is an annual 8-day women's royal ceremony in Eswatini with distinctive vocal and processional music.
genres.note: The Reed Dance (Umhlanga) is a national ceremony of Eswatini with countrywide participation held annually at the royal residence in Lobamba.

genres.name: Makhoyane
genres.start_label: The makhoyane is a traditional Swati musical bow played by women as a solo instrument for personal and social expression.
genres.note: Makhoyane is a traditional Swazi single-string instrument concentrated in the central and lowveld regions of Eswatini, used in personal song composition.

genres.name: Isitolotolo
genres.start_label: Isitolotolo is a traditional Swati jaw harp, a small metal instrument used for personal music within the Swazi indigenous instrument repertoire.
genres.note: Isitolotolo is a traditional instrument and associated music from Eswatini, practiced in the central Hhohho and Manzini regions of the highland kingdom.

genres.name: Bikutsi
genres.start_label: Bikutsi emerged as a recognizable popular genre in the mid-20th century from Beti traditional dance music. International profile developed from the 1980s through artists including
genres.note: Bikutsi is Cameroonian dance music developed from Beti and Ewondo traditions around Yaoundé. It became popular in West Africa during the mid-twentieth century.

genres.name: Makossa
genres.start_label: Makossa originated in Douala in the 1950s and achieved international recognition in 1972 through Manu Dibango's 'Soul Makossa'.
genres.note: Makossa developed in Douala, Cameroon, as a dance-oriented popular style. Its ensembles feature electric bass, guitars, percussion, brass, lead voice, and answering singers.

genres.name: Lam Salavane
genres.start_label: Garland (1998) documents lam salavane as a living southern Lao repartee tradition with documented regional styles; no origin date given.
genres.note: Lam salavane is a Lao-language song genre of southern Laos sung by Lao and Mon-Khmer performers. Accompaniment ranges from solo khene mouth organ to mixed instrumental ensembles.

sources.citation: Terry E. Miller and Sean Williams, eds., The Garland Encyclopedia of World Music, vol. 4: Southeast Asia, Garland Publishing, 1998.

genres.name: Lao Classical Music
genres.start_label: Garland (1998) records Lao classical music as a revived court tradition; post-1975 suppression followed by revival documented. Dissertation research on Vientiane court music conduc
genres.note: Lao classical music includes court-associated ensembles and theatrical repertory linked to Luang Prabang and the Fine Arts School in Vientiane. It is locally distinguished from lam song traditions.

sources.citation: Terry E. Miller and Sean Williams, eds., The Garland Encyclopedia of World Music, vol. 4: Southeast Asia, Garland Publishing, 1998.

genres.name: Li-ke theater
genres.start_label: Li-ke theater arrived in Laos around 1940 from Siam and has been used alongside Mor lam in entertainment contexts.
genres.note: Like theater is a popular musical theater form from central Laos, centered in Vientiane and the lowland Mekong communities of the capital region.

genres.name: Ikinimba
genres.start_label: Ikinimba are praise songs for cattle performed during ceremonies, historically associated with the long-horned Inyambo cattle of Tutsi pastoral culture.
genres.note: Ikinimba is a traditional Rwandan community drum tradition originating among the communities of Burera and Gicumbi in northern Rwanda.

genres.name: Nhac Le
genres.start_label: Garland (1998) documents nhac le as a living Vietnamese ritual tradition with regional variants; audio example track 8 (p. 483). The Hue court began restoring ritual music prior to
genres.note: Nhạc lễ is southern Vietnamese instrumental music for ceremonies and celebrations. Its ensembles grew from earlier central and south-central practices and influenced later southern repertories.

sources.citation: Terry E. Miller and Sean Williams, eds., The Garland Encyclopedia of World Music, vol. 4: Southeast Asia, Garland Publishing, 1998.

genres.name: Chau Van
genres.start_label: Garland (1998) documents chau van as a suppressed but surviving ritual tradition; post-1975 ban documented. No origin date assigned.
genres.note: Chầu văn is Vietnamese ritual music linked to spirit-medium ceremonies, especially in northern and central regions. Singing, moon-shaped lute, gongs, and drums accompany the rites.

sources.citation: Terry E. Miller and Sean Williams, eds., The Garland Encyclopedia of World Music, vol. 4: Southeast Asia, Garland Publishing, 1998.

genres.name: Tân nhạc
genres.start_label: Tân nhạc emerged in the 1930s as a Western-influenced Vietnamese popular music using Western notation and harmony. Key artists include Đặng Thế Phong and Văn Cao.
genres.note: Tân nhạc (new music) emerged in Hanoi in the 1930s as the first Vietnamese modern popular music movement, fusing Western harmony with Vietnamese pentatonic scales.

genres.name: Nhạc đỏ / Nhạc vàng
genres.start_label: Nhạc đỏ (revolutionary) and Nhạc vàng (sentimental) developed as politically opposed popular music traditions from the 1950s through 1975. After reunification, Nhạc vàng was suppre
genres.note: Nhạc đỏ (revolutionary music from northern Vietnam) and nhạc vàng (sentimental pop from the southern Republic) are opposed popular traditions reunified in the post-1975 canon.

genres.name: V-pop
genres.start_label: V-pop emerged from the 1990s onward following Đổi Mới economic reform, blending Western pop production with Vietnamese lyrics. Artists include Mỹ Tâm and Sơn Tùng M-TP.
genres.note: V-pop is Vietnam's contemporary pop music industry, centered in Ho Chi Minh City in southern Vietnam, drawing on Korean, American, and Chinese pop production styles.

genres.name: Askiya
genres.start_label: Sultanova lists Askiya as one of Uzbekistan's five UNESCO ICH nominations; no precise origin date established.
genres.note: Askiya is a competitive verbal wit tradition and musical performance form from the Fergana Valley in eastern Uzbekistan, particularly around Andijan and Namangan.

sources.citation: Razia Sultanova and Megan Rancier, eds., Turkic Soundscapes: From Shamanic Voices to Hip-Hop, Routledge, 2018.

genres.name: Uzbek estrada
genres.start_label: The Central Asia Further Reading bibliography documents scholarly attention to Uzbek estrada from the Soviet period (1930s–1980s) through post-independence transformation.
genres.note: Uzbek estrada is popular entertainment music centered in Tashkent, the capital in northeastern Uzbekistan, combining variety show formats with local melodic traditions.

sources.citation: Music of Central Asia: Further Reading, Listening, and Viewing, official companion, 2017, musicofcentralasia.org.

genres.name: Tuareg Takumba
genres.start_label: Documented by Garland (1998) as emerging in Niger in the 1970s with drought-era migration.
genres.note: Takumba is a Tuareg string music tradition from the Agadez and Aïr massif region of northern Niger, associated with nomadic Tuareg communities.

sources.citation: Ruth M. Stone, ed., The Garland Encyclopedia of World Music, vol. 1: Africa, Garland Publishing, 1998.

genres.name: Hausa griot tradition
genres.kind: court praise music and oral history tradition
genres.start_label: Major Hausa cultural institution of long standing; no precise origin date established.
genres.note: The Hausa griot tradition of praise-singing and court music is centered in the cities of Zinder, Maradi, and Dosso in southern Niger.

genres.name: Zarma-Songhai music
genres.start_label: Traditional music of the Zarma and Songhai peoples; no precise origin date established.
genres.note: Zarma-Songhai music is a vocal and percussion tradition from the Niamey and western Niger River valley region, home of the Zarma and Songhai peoples.

genres.name: Zinli
genres.start_label: Traditional voodoo ceremony music of the Fon people of southern Benin; no precise origin date established.
genres.note: Zinli is a Fon ceremonial music from southern Benin, played on hourglass tension drums at funerary and vodun ritual ceremonies in the Abomey and Ouidah area.

genres.name: Akinta
genres.start_label: Traditional ceremonial music form; no precise origin date established.
genres.note: Akinta is a Yoruba-influenced warrior music tradition from southern Benin, performed with drums and iron bells during ceremonies in the Porto-Novo and coastal areas.

genres.name: Akohoun
genres.start_label: Traditional ceremony-linked musical form; no precise origin date established.
genres.note: Akohoun is a Fon music tradition from southern Benin, performed at royal ceremonies and vodun rituals by specialist musicians in the Abomey court area.

genres.name: Tchinkoume
genres.start_label: Traditional Beninese ceremonial music form; no precise origin date established.
genres.note: Tchinkoume is a traditional music form from the Fon people of southern Benin, characterized by polyrhythmic drumming and communal vocal participation.

genres.name: Toba
genres.start_label: Traditional ceremonial drumming and vocal tradition; no precise origin date established.
genres.note: Toba is a traditional percussion and vocal music from southern Benin, associated with Fon ceremonial practices in the historical Abomey kingdom area.

genres.name: Agbotchébou
genres.start_label: Traditional Beninese voodoo ceremony music; no precise origin date established.
genres.note: Agbotchebou is a Fon ceremonial drumming tradition from southern Benin, linked to vodun practices and the royal courts of the Abomey plateau.

genres.name: IWE
genres.start_label: Traditional Yoruba/Kétou ceremonial music tradition; no precise origin date established.
genres.note: Iwe is a song tradition of the Fon people of southern Benin, performed during harvest festivals and communal celebrations in the coastal zone.

genres.name: Dondang Sayang
genres.start_label: Garland (1998) documents dondang sayang as a living genre among Singapore Peranakans; no origin date given.
genres.note: Dondang Sayang is an improvised Malay sung-poetry form that spread from Melaka to Singapore. Performers exchange pantun verses over a small instrumental accompaniment.

sources.citation: Terry E. Miller and Sean Williams, eds., The Garland Encyclopedia of World Music, vol. 4: Southeast Asia, Garland Publishing, 1998.

genres.name: Getai
genres.start_label: Garland (1998) documents getai as a contemporary Singaporean tradition active in the late 1990s; no earlier origin date established.
genres.note: Getai is a Singaporean live song-stage tradition especially associated with the seventh lunar month. Performances present popular songs, electric accompaniment, and comic commentary.

sources.citation: Terry E. Miller and Sean Williams, eds., The Garland Encyclopedia of World Music, vol. 4: Southeast Asia, Garland Publishing, 1998.

genres.name: Nabaṭī
genres.start_label: Entry traces nabaṭī to a pre-Islamic age; its Gulf spread through migration is documented.
genres.note: Nabaṭī is vernacular Arabian poetry heard in the United Arab Emirates and other Gulf communities. Its sung and recited forms address praise, love, loss, and tribal life.

sources.citation: Richard C. Jankowsky, vol. ed., Bloomsbury Encyclopedia of Popular Music of the World, vol. X: Genres: Middle East and North Africa, Bloomsbury Academic, 2015.

genres.name: ʿArḍa
genres.start_label: Entry documents contemporary ceremonial performance but gives no Bahrain-specific origin date.
genres.note: ʿArḍa is a Gulf communal song and sword-dance performed at celebrations and public events. Bahrain has local variants of the Najdi form, with men singing in facing lines to drums.

sources.citation: Richard C. Jankowsky, vol. ed., Bloomsbury Encyclopedia of Popular Music of the World, vol. X: Genres: Middle East and North Africa, Bloomsbury Academic, 2015.

genres.name: Ṣawt
genres.start_label: Entry dates Gulf ṣawt to the mid-to-late nineteenth century and documents continued early-twenty-first-century performance.
genres.note: Ṣawt is upper Gulf art music strongly associated with Bahrain and Kuwait. A singer typically accompanies himself on the ʿūd while a mirwās drum supplies the rhythm.

sources.citation: Richard C. Jankowsky, vol. ed., Bloomsbury Encyclopedia of Popular Music of the World, vol. X: Genres: Middle East and North Africa, Bloomsbury Academic, 2015.

genres.name: Nabaṭī
genres.start_label: Entry traces nabaṭī to a pre-Islamic age; its Gulf spread through migration is documented.
genres.note: Nabaṭī is vernacular poetry from Arabia's central plateau that spread into Bahrain and other Gulf communities. Its poems may be chanted or sung, alone or with rebāba accompaniment.

sources.citation: Richard C. Jankowsky, vol. ed., Bloomsbury Encyclopedia of Popular Music of the World, vol. X: Genres: Middle East and North Africa, Bloomsbury Academic, 2015.

genres.name: Dithlaka
genres.start_label: Dithlaka are traditional transverse copper tube/flute instruments of Botswana played in ensemble.
genres.note: Dithlaka are traditional Tswana rhythm sticks used in music from southeastern Botswana, particularly in communities around Gaborone and the eastern hardveld.

genres.name: Setapa
genres.start_label: Setapa is a Tswana community dance tradition combining music and oral narrative, performed at social ceremonies.
genres.note: Setapa is a traditional Tswana dance-music from southeastern Botswana, performed at social gatherings in the Gaborone and eastern districts.

genres.name: Zajal
genres.start_label: Entry describes contemporary mashriq practice; classical form dates from twelfth-century Andalusia.
genres.note: Zajal is a Levantine tradition of improvised sung poetry in colloquial Arabic. Syrian rural and Bedouin performers shape verses within established rhyme schemes, often with a responding chorus.

sources.citation: Richard C. Jankowsky, vol. ed., Bloomsbury Encyclopedia of Popular Music of the World, vol. X: Genres: Middle East and North Africa, Bloomsbury Academic, 2015.

genres.name: Badawī
genres.start_label: Entry describes badawī as an Arab folk genre of nomadic and settled Bedouin populations across the Arab world.
genres.note: Badawī music belongs to Arab Bedouin song and storytelling traditions across the Levant, including Syria. Its poetic subjects include love, generosity, and courage.

sources.citation: Richard C. Jankowsky, vol. ed., Bloomsbury Encyclopedia of Popular Music of the World, vol. X: Genres: Middle East and North Africa, Bloomsbury Academic, 2015.

genres.name: Mawwāl
genres.start_label: Entry traces the genre to Abbasid-era practices and documents its spread from Egypt throughout the Arab world, with Syrian performers among its leading figures.
genres.note: Mawwāl gives a Syrian soloist room for unmetered melodic improvisation over short poetic texts. Ṣabāḥ Fakhrī was a notable Syrian performer of the form.

sources.citation: Richard C. Jankowsky, vol. ed., Bloomsbury Encyclopedia of Popular Music of the World, vol. X: Genres: Middle East and North Africa, Bloomsbury Academic, 2015.

genres.name: Ṭarab
genres.start_label: Entry describes ṭarab peaking in the second half of the twentieth century in Egypt and the eastern Mediterranean.
genres.note: Ṭarab is the emotional engagement created by skilled Arab singing and instrumental performance. Syrian singer Ṣabāḥ Fakhrī was an important exponent of this art-music approach.

sources.citation: Richard C. Jankowsky, vol. ed., Bloomsbury Encyclopedia of Popular Music of the World, vol. X: Genres: Middle East and North Africa, Bloomsbury Academic, 2015.

genres.name: Bashraf
genres.start_label: Entry traces bashraf to Ottoman court music around the sixteenth century and documents Aleppine composers in the nineteenth–twentieth centuries.
genres.note: Bashraf is an instrumental composition used in Ottoman and Arab classical suites. Aleppo adopted the form and became a center for Arab composers working in it.

sources.citation: Richard C. Jankowsky, vol. ed., Bloomsbury Encyclopedia of Popular Music of the World, vol. X: Genres: Middle East and North Africa, Bloomsbury Academic, 2015.

genres.name: Dūlāb
genres.start_label: Entry describes dūlāb as a traditional Arab music genre of unknown origin used as an introductory prelude.
genres.note: Dūlāb is a brief Arab instrumental prelude that introduces a song's maqām, or melodic mode. An Aleppine example in the Ḥijāz mode shows its place in Syrian classical performance.

sources.citation: Richard C. Jankowsky, vol. ed., Bloomsbury Encyclopedia of Popular Music of the World, vol. X: Genres: Middle East and North Africa, Bloomsbury Academic, 2015.

genres.name: Samāʿī
genres.start_label: Entry traces samāʿī to Ottoman court music around the sixteenth century and documents Aleppine and Egyptian composers in the nineteenth–twentieth centuries.
genres.note: Samāʿī is a composed instrumental genre in Arab and Turkish classical music, with alternating sections and a recurring refrain. Aleppine composers developed notable examples.

sources.citation: Richard C. Jankowsky, vol. ed., Bloomsbury Encyclopedia of Popular Music of the World, vol. X: Genres: Middle East and North Africa, Bloomsbury Academic, 2015.

genres.name: Ṭaqṭūqa
genres.start_label: Entry describes the genre as pioneered in Egypt at the end of the nineteenth century and adopted widely in Aleppo; it peaked around the mid-twentieth century.
genres.note: Ṭaqṭūqa is a concise Arab song form with a refrain between verses. Aleppo singers added it to their repertoires as the style spread beyond Egypt.

sources.citation: Richard C. Jankowsky, vol. ed., Bloomsbury Encyclopedia of Popular Music of the World, vol. X: Genres: Middle East and North Africa, Bloomsbury Academic, 2015.

genres.name: Amadinda Xylophone Music
genres.start_label: Pre-colonial court tradition documented by Garland (1998) as a living Buganda xylophone practice.
genres.note: Amadinda is a Baganda log-xylophone practice in which three musicians combine interlocking parts on a twelve-key instrument. Two players establish patterns while the third draws out a higher part.

sources.citation: Ruth M. Stone, ed., The Garland Encyclopedia of World Music, vol. 1: Africa, Garland Publishing, 1998.

genres.name: Akadinda
genres.start_label: Pre-colonial royal court tradition documented by Garland (1998).
genres.note: Akadinda is a large court xylophone formerly played in the Buganda ruler's palace ensemble. Its performance could require a team of six musicians.

sources.citation: Ruth M. Stone, ed., The Garland Encyclopedia of World Music, vol. 1: Africa, Garland Publishing, 1998.

genres.name: Baakisimba
genres.start_label: Pre-colonial court tradition documented by Garland (1998) as the 'national' Baganda dance.
genres.note: Baakisimba is a Baganda feast dance historically linked to the kabaka's court. Its steps are traditionally interpreted as planting plantain shoots.

sources.citation: Ruth M. Stone, ed., The Garland Encyclopedia of World Music, vol. 1: Africa, Garland Publishing, 1998.

genres.name: Enswezi Cult Music
genres.start_label: Traditional healing practice documented by Garland (1998) in southeastern Uganda.
genres.note: Enswezi music accompanies spirit-healing rites in Busoga, Uganda. Interlocking drums, sung invocations, rattles, and women's voices through gourd kazoos support the ceremony.

sources.citation: Ruth M. Stone, ed., The Garland Encyclopedia of World Music, vol. 1: Africa, Garland Publishing, 1998.

genres.name: Bwola
genres.start_label: Traditional Acholi court practice documented by Garland (1998).
genres.note: Bwola is a royal drum dance of the Acholi people of northern Uganda, performed in the Gulu and Kitgum districts at ceremonies and royal celebrations.

sources.citation: Ruth M. Stone, ed., The Garland Encyclopedia of World Music, vol. 1: Africa, Garland Publishing, 1998.

genres.name: Abayudaya Jewish Liturgical Music
genres.start_label: Community founded by Semei Kakungulu in the early 1920s; first Hebrew contact in 1926; music incorporates Basoga ngoma, adungu harp songs, and Bagisu circumcision song styles refra
genres.note: Abayudaya Jewish liturgical and related songs in Uganda use Luganda and Hebrew texts. Performers adapt local drumming, adungu harp, and village guitar practices to Jewish worship and biblical themes.

sources.citation: Ruth M. Stone (ed.), The Garland Handbook of African Music, 2nd ed., Routledge, 2008, pp. 312-325.

genres.name: Maqām (Kurdish)
genres.start_label: Entry states the mystical tradition of the Ahl-e Haqq dates from the thirteenth century; secularization began in the 1970s and international distribution via World Music recordings
genres.note: Kurdish maqām here refers to the sacred Yarsan repertoire shared across Iranian and Iraqi Kurdistan and beyond. Tanbur lute playing and oral transmission are central to its devotional practice.

sources.citation: Richard C. Jankowsky, vol. ed., Bloomsbury Encyclopedia of Popular Music of the World, vol. X: Genres: Middle East and North Africa, Bloomsbury Academic, 2015.

genres.name: Muwwal
genres.start_label: Muwwal is a regional folk singing style documented as a living rural practice in Iraq, distinct from the urban Iraqi Maqam tradition. Precise historical dating is unresolved.
genres.note: Muwwal is an Iraqi vocal improvisation genre associated with Wasit and Baghdad in central Iraq, based on classical Arabic and local maqam melodic modes.

genres.name: Fusion in Morocco
genres.start_label: Entry describes Moroccan fusion as a modern popular genre.
genres.note: Moroccan fusion groups combine local traditional and popular styles with international sounds such as rock, reggae, hip-hop, jazz, and salsa. The style grew commercially in the early 2000s.

sources.citation: Richard C. Jankowsky, vol. ed., Bloomsbury Encyclopedia of Popular Music of the World, vol. X: Genres: Middle East and North Africa, Bloomsbury Academic, 2015.

genres.name: Shaʿbī (Moroccan)
genres.start_label: Entry places Moroccan shaʿbī's modern form in the 1950s–1960s (ʿAbd al-Wahhāb Dūkalī, Ḥamīd Zahīr) and its reinvigoration in 1971 (Nāss al-Ghiwān).
genres.note: Moroccan shaʿbī is a commercially popular umbrella for modernized Arabophone regional styles. Its recording history grew with local cassette production during the 1970s.

sources.citation: Richard C. Jankowsky, vol. ed., Bloomsbury Encyclopedia of Popular Music of the World, vol. X: Genres: Middle East and North Africa, Bloomsbury Academic, 2015.

genres.name: Āla (Andalusian music)
genres.start_label: Entry traces the tradition to Andalusian refugees who brought it to North Africa between the tenth and seventeenth centuries.
genres.note: Āla is the Moroccan school of North African Andalusian music. Its nubah suites organize sung poetry and instrumental passages around shared melodic modes.

sources.citation: Richard C. Jankowsky, vol. ed., Bloomsbury Encyclopedia of Popular Music of the World, vol. X: Genres: Middle East and North Africa, Bloomsbury Academic, 2015.

genres.name: Arab-Andalusian Nubah
genres.start_label: Tradition brought to Morocco after the Reconquista (post-1492); documented by Garland (1998) as a living classical suite tradition.
genres.note: Moroccan nubah music continues an Andalusian suite repertory in schools associated with Fez and Tetuan. Each suite joins vocal and instrumental movements in set rhythmic modes.

sources.citation: Ruth M. Stone, ed., The Garland Encyclopedia of World Music, vol. 1: Africa, Garland Publishing, 1998.

genres.name: Azri
genres.start_label: Documented by Garland (1998) as gaining popularity in the early radio era; broadly mid-20th century.
genres.note: Azri is Moroccan urban popular music influenced by Middle Eastern broadcasts and by Moroccan, European, and American styles. It became prominent during the early radio era.

sources.citation: Ruth M. Stone, ed., The Garland Encyclopedia of World Music, vol. 1: Africa, Garland Publishing, 1998.

genres.name: Jali/Griot kora tradition
genres.start_label: The jali/griot tradition is of deep historical standing in West Africa; no single origin date is established for The Gambia.
genres.note: The jali griot tradition with kora is central to Mandinka musical culture, concentrated in the western division around Banjul and the Gambia River communities.

sources.citation: Ruth M. Stone, ed., The Garland Encyclopedia of World Music, vol. 1: Africa, Garland Publishing, 1998.

genres.name: Campus folk songs
genres.start_label: Cheng traces the movement to Hu Defu's 1972 concert, the 1975 campus folk song events, and the subsequent genre formation through the late 1970s.
genres.note: Taiwan's campus folk songs grew from the 1970s movement to sing locally written music, associated with Hu Defu and the 'Sing Our Own Song' slogan. The style also influenced later mainland Chinese youth culture.

sources.citation: Ya-Hui Cheng, The Evolution of Chinese Popular Music: Modernization and Globalization, 1927 to the Present, Routledge, 2023.

genres.name: Taiwanese rock
genres.start_label: Cheng places Taiwanese rock in the context of the 1980s campus folk song aftermath, with figures like Luo Dayou and Rock Records as defining forces.
genres.note: Taiwanese rock developed partly from the island's campus folk-song movement. Luo Dayou and Rock Records helped establish its place in Taiwan's popular-music industry.

sources.citation: Ya-Hui Cheng, The Evolution of Chinese Popular Music: Modernization and Globalization, 1927 to the Present, Routledge, 2023.

genres.name: Mandopop
genres.start_label: Cheng identifies Taiwan as the Mando-pop center in the 1980s; the 1990s saw major multinational labels establishing Taiwanese operations to capture the greater Chinese market.
genres.note: Taiwan became a major production and distribution center for Mandarin-language popular music from the 1980s. Its recording industry served Chinese-language audiences beyond the island.

sources.citation: Ya-Hui Cheng, The Evolution of Chinese Popular Music: Modernization and Globalization, 1927 to the Present, Routledge, 2023.

genres.name: Kafi
genres.start_label: Garland (2000) names Sufi poets who used the kafi form, including Sheikh Fariduddin Masud Ganj-i Shakar (d. 1265 CE). Living tradition documented with contemporary performers Patha
genres.note: Kafi is a Sufi devotional song and poetic form prominent in Sindh and Punjab. Singers use refrains and may draw on the verse of regional poet-saints, with accompaniment varying by performer.

sources.citation: Alison Arnold, ed., The Garland Encyclopedia of World Music, vol. 5: South Asia: The Indian Subcontinent, Garland Publishing, 2000.

genres.name: Ghazal
genres.start_label: Ghazal is a classical Urdu and Persian poetic song form consisting of rhyming couplets on themes of love and loss. Pakistan has been a major centre of Ghazal performance, with key
genres.note: The ghazal is a poetic form often addressing love, longing, and separation; sung ghazals are an important South Asian musical practice. The form spread into the subcontinent through Persianate court culture.

genres.name: Nabaṭī
genres.start_label: Entry traces nabaṭī to a pre-Islamic age; its Gulf spread through migration is documented.
genres.note: Nabaṭī is vernacular Arabian poetry maintained in Kuwait and the wider Gulf. Singers may deliver its verse unaccompanied or with a rebāba bowed string instrument.

sources.citation: Richard C. Jankowsky, vol. ed., Bloomsbury Encyclopedia of Popular Music of the World, vol. X: Genres: Middle East and North Africa, Bloomsbury Academic, 2015.

genres.name: Akazehe
genres.start_label: Akazehe is a Burundian women's tradition using small whistle instruments in social celebrations.
genres.note: Akazehe is a female vocal genre from central Burundi, performed by women in antiphonal choral form during ceremonies, with Ngozi province as a primary site.

genres.name: Kulintang
genres.start_label: Garland (1998) documents kulintang as an established classical/ensemble tradition of southern Philippines; Garland notes it is 'not locally promoted as a classical music' despite c
genres.note: Kulintang is a gong-chime ensemble tradition of the southern Philippines. Its central instrument arranges tuned bronze pot gongs in a horizontal row within a larger percussion ensemble.

sources.citation: Terry E. Miller and Sean Williams, eds., The Garland Encyclopedia of World Music, vol. 4: Southeast Asia, Garland Publishing, 1998.

genres.name: Harana
genres.start_label: Garland (1998) documents harana as a living Philippine serenade tradition; Spanish loanword origin noted; no precise date given.
genres.note: Harana is the Philippine serenade tradition, encompassing repertoires among Tagalog, Pampango, Bikolano, Ilocano, and Pangasinan communities. Tagalog serenades follow a sequence of songs.

sources.citation: Terry E. Miller and Sean Williams, eds., The Garland Encyclopedia of World Music, vol. 4: Southeast Asia, Garland Publishing, 1998.

genres.name: OPM (Original Pilipino Music)
genres.start_label: OPM emerged in the 1970s as a deliberate category of Philippine popular music in Filipino languages, as an alternative to imported music. Artists include Freddie Aguilar, Sharon Cu
genres.note: Original Pilipino Music (OPM) is the popular music of the Philippines, centered in Manila and the Luzon recording industry in the northern part of the country.

genres.name: Palestinian resistance music
genres.kind: popular music genre / protest music tradition
genres.start_label: Palestinian hip-hop and resistance music emerged from the 1990s onward; DAM is documented as the first Palestinian hip-hop group.
genres.note: Palestinian resistance music is an explicitly trans-territorial tradition documented across the West Bank, Gaza, and diaspora communities, expressing national identity.

genres.name: Turkish makam
genres.start_label: Öztürk documents makam theory from 15th-century Ottoman treatises; the tradition continues in contemporary Turkish music education and performance.
genres.note: Turkish makam organizes melodic movement in Ottoman and later Turkish classical music. Written accounts of the system reach back to the fifteenth century.

sources.citation: Razia Sultanova and Megan Rancier, eds., Turkic Soundscapes: From Shamanic Voices to Hip-Hop, Routledge, 2018.

genres.name: Semah
genres.kind: devotional ritual music and movement genre
genres.start_label: Sultanova identifies Semah as one of Turkey's five UNESCO ICH nominations; the tradition's pre-Ottoman Sufi roots make precise dating difficult.
genres.note: Semah joins rhythmic movement and saz lute music in the Alevi-Bektaşi cem ritual. Women and men perform side by side, with local musical and rhythmic variations across Turkey.

sources.citation: Razia Sultanova and Megan Rancier, eds., Turkic Soundscapes: From Shamanic Voices to Hip-Hop, Routledge, 2018.

genres.name: Gazel
genres.start_label: Entry describes the gazel as fixed in its current form in the twentieth century and accounting for about a quarter of all Turkish sound recordings in the early twentieth century.
genres.note: Gazel is a Turkish vocal improvisation based on rhymed poetic couplets. A singer elaborates the text melodically, often adding expressive vocables between lines.

sources.citation: Richard C. Jankowsky, vol. ed., Bloomsbury Encyclopedia of Popular Music of the World, vol. X: Genres: Middle East and North Africa, Bloomsbury Academic, 2015.

genres.name: Türkü
genres.start_label: Türkü is the oral folk song tradition of the Anatolian countryside, predating the Ottoman period and continuing as a living tradition. Urban revival documented from mid-20th centur
genres.note: Türkü is the collective name for Turkish regional folk songs, a tradition spanning every Anatolian province with distinct local repertoires throughout the country.

genres.name: Özgün Müzik
genres.kind: popular music genre / protest folk hybrid
genres.start_label: Özgün Müzik emerged in Turkey in the early 1980s as a politically engaged folk-popular hybrid in response to the September 1980 military coup.
genres.note: Özgün müzik is a politically engaged folk-pop genre that emerged in Istanbul and İzmir in the 1970s, drawing on Anatolian folk tunes with leftist lyrical content.

genres.name: Dan Ge Performance Music
genres.start_label: Long-established Dan institution; documented through fieldwork in 1997; incorporates popular music styles such as zouglou in contemporary performance.
genres.note: Dan Ge performances combine masked dance with drumming and singing in western Côte d'Ivoire. Their repertory includes dance songs, praise songs, and funeral laments.

sources.citation: Ruth M. Stone (ed.), The Garland Handbook of African Music, 2nd ed., Routledge, 2008, pp. 216-237.

genres.name: Gnakpa
genres.start_label: Named alongside zouglou and zaiiko as Ivorian popular music and dance styles of the 1990s.
genres.note: Gnakpa is a Côte d'Ivoire popular music and dance style documented in the 1990s. Its rhythms and steps were taken up by some Dan Ge masked performers.

sources.citation: Ruth M. Stone (ed.), The Garland Handbook of African Music, 2nd ed., Routledge, 2008, p. 225.

genres.name: Jarigan
genres.start_label: Garland (2000) documents jarigan as a living Bangladesh folk narrative genre; no origin date given.
genres.note: Jarigan is a devotional folk song tradition found across Bangladesh and into the adjacent Indian Bengal, performed in call-and-response group singing at rural gatherings.

sources.citation: Alison Arnold, ed., The Garland Encyclopedia of World Music, vol. 5: South Asia: The Indian Subcontinent, Garland Publishing, 2000.

genres.name: Pala Kirtan
genres.start_label: Garland (2000) documents pala kirtan as originating in the fifteenth–sixteenth centuries in Bengal; active tradition documented as of 2000.
genres.note: Pala kirtan is a narrative devotional singing tradition originating in the Mymensingh region of northern Bangladesh, with performers alternating solo and chorus parts.

sources.citation: Alison Arnold, ed., The Garland Encyclopedia of World Music, vol. 5: South Asia: The Indian Subcontinent, Garland Publishing, 2000.

genres.name: Mawwāl
genres.start_label: Entry documents Egyptian artists performing mawwāl from the beginning of the twentieth century and names Muḥammad ʿAbd al-Wahhāb among its contributors.
genres.note: Mawwāl is an unmetered Arab vocal improvisation over colloquial poetry, sometimes opening a longer song suite. Egyptian performers used it to display melodic invention within a maqām.

sources.citation: Richard C. Jankowsky, vol. ed., Bloomsbury Encyclopedia of Popular Music of the World, vol. X: Genres: Middle East and North Africa, Bloomsbury Academic, 2015.

genres.name: Ṭarab
genres.start_label: Entry describes ṭarab as peaking in the second half of the twentieth century in Egypt and the eastern Mediterranean.
genres.note: Ṭarab is the emotional intensity sought in Arab art music through poetry, melodic nuance, and improvisation. Egypt was a major center of its twentieth-century singers, including Umm Kulthūm.

sources.citation: Richard C. Jankowsky, vol. ed., Bloomsbury Encyclopedia of Popular Music of the World, vol. X: Genres: Middle East and North Africa, Bloomsbury Academic, 2015.

genres.name: Bashraf
genres.start_label: Entry traces bashraf to Ottoman court music around the sixteenth century and documents its popularity in Cairo from the nineteenth century.
genres.note: Bashraf is an Ottoman-derived instrumental form within the Arab classical suite. It entered Cairo's art-music life and often served as part of a longer medley.

sources.citation: Richard C. Jankowsky, vol. ed., Bloomsbury Encyclopedia of Popular Music of the World, vol. X: Genres: Middle East and North Africa, Bloomsbury Academic, 2015.

genres.name: Samāʿī
genres.start_label: Entry documents the 1932 Cairo Arab Music Conference as a key moment and names nineteenth-to-twentieth-century Egyptian composers.
genres.note: Samāʿī is an instrumental Arab and Turkish classical form whose sections return to a common refrain. Egyptian composers developed Arab examples during the twentieth century.

sources.citation: Richard C. Jankowsky, vol. ed., Bloomsbury Encyclopedia of Popular Music of the World, vol. X: Genres: Middle East and North Africa, Bloomsbury Academic, 2015.

genres.name: Ṭaqṭūqa
genres.start_label: Entry states the genre was pioneered by Muḥammad ʿAlī Luʿba at the end of the nineteenth century and peaked around the mid-twentieth century in Egypt.
genres.note: Ṭaqṭūqa is a short Egyptian vocal form built around a refrain repeated between verses. It rose with early recording and cinema and helped shape the modern Arab popular song.

sources.citation: Richard C. Jankowsky, vol. ed., Bloomsbury Encyclopedia of Popular Music of the World, vol. X: Genres: Middle East and North Africa, Bloomsbury Academic, 2015.

genres.name: Qaṣīda
genres.start_label: Entry dates the first Egyptian sung qaṣāʾid to Salamah Ḥijāzī (1852–1917) at the beginning of the twentieth century.
genres.note: Qaṣīda sets formal Arabic poetry to singing, often on themes of love, patriotism, or spiritual reflection. Egyptian artists including Umm Kulthūm made it a central art-song form.

sources.citation: Richard C. Jankowsky, vol. ed., Bloomsbury Encyclopedia of Popular Music of the World, vol. X: Genres: Middle East and North Africa, Bloomsbury Academic, 2015.

genres.name: Ughniyya (Eastern Arab)
genres.start_label: Entry dates the genre's consolidation to the mid-twentieth century when the waṣla medley format was replaced by the shorter song.
genres.note: Ughniyya is a modern Arab short-song category that expanded as older suites and improvisatory forms lost ground. Cairo's recording and music industry helped circulate this song format.

sources.citation: Richard C. Jankowsky, vol. ed., Bloomsbury Encyclopedia of Popular Music of the World, vol. X: Genres: Middle East and North Africa, Bloomsbury Academic, 2015.

genres.name: Shabābī
genres.start_label: Entry dates shabābī's emergence to Cairo's recording studios in the 1980s and describes its maturation through the 1990s with videoclips.
genres.note: Shabābī is Egyptian youth-oriented popular music that grew in Cairo's recording studios in the 1980s. Its short songs use catchy refrains, modern production, and influences from international pop.

sources.citation: Richard C. Jankowsky, vol. ed., Bloomsbury Encyclopedia of Popular Music of the World, vol. X: Genres: Middle East and North Africa, Bloomsbury Academic, 2015.

genres.name: Nubian Ceremonial Music
genres.start_label: Pre-colonial tradition documented by Garland (1998) as a living Nubian practice in Egypt.
genres.note: Nubian music is the traditional and contemporary music of the Nubian people, rooted in the Aswan region of far southern Egypt.

sources.citation: Ruth M. Stone, ed., The Garland Encyclopedia of World Music, vol. 1: Africa, Garland Publishing, 1998.

genres.name: Zajal
genres.start_label: Entry describes contemporary semi-improvised zajal practice in the mashriq including Jordan; the classical strophic form dates from twelfth-century Andalusia.
genres.note: Zajal is a Levantine practice of sung, partly improvised colloquial poetry. Jordanian rural and Bedouin performers use set rhyme patterns and can sing with a responding chorus.

sources.citation: Richard C. Jankowsky, vol. ed., Bloomsbury Encyclopedia of Popular Music of the World, vol. X: Genres: Middle East and North Africa, Bloomsbury Academic, 2015.

genres.name: Badawī
genres.start_label: Entry describes badawī as an Arab folk genre of nomadic and settled Bedouin populations; Jordan's state radio broadcast context is mentioned as a key modern platform.
genres.note: Badawī is Arab Bedouin song and poetic storytelling, carried across modern national borders. Jordanian performers include singer and instrumentalist ʿAbdū Mūsā.

sources.citation: Richard C. Jankowsky, vol. ed., Bloomsbury Encyclopedia of Popular Music of the World, vol. X: Genres: Middle East and North Africa, Bloomsbury Academic, 2015.

genres.name: Simsimiyya
genres.kind: folk tradition / port community lyre music
genres.start_label: Simsimiyya is a five-string lyre tradition documented in the Aqaba port community of Jordan and the Suez Canal area of Egypt; an active folk music practice of fishing and port comm
genres.note: Simsimiyya is a lyre tradition from the southern port city of Aqaba, associated with coastal and fishing communities of the Red Sea shore of Jordan.

genres.name: Amman indie scene
genres.kind: urban popular music / independent music scene
genres.start_label: An independent rock and alternative music scene developed in Amman from the mid-2000s, with venues such as Hangar and the Rainbow Street area as key gathering points.
genres.note: Amman indie is an independent urban music scene centered in Amman, the capital in the northwestern corridor of Jordan, active since the 2000s.

genres.name: Ewe Traditional Music
genres.start_label: Pre-colonial tradition documented by Garland (1998) in the Ewe article with explicit reference to Togo.
genres.note: Ewe traditional music is the ensemble drumming and vocal tradition of the Ewe people from the Maritime region around Lomé in southern Togo.

sources.citation: Ruth M. Stone, ed., The Garland Encyclopedia of World Music, vol. 1: Africa, Garland Publishing, 1998.

genres.name: Libyan Gnawa
genres.start_label: Pre-colonial tradition documented by Garland (1998) as an active Libyan practice.
genres.note: Gnawa music in Libya is practiced by communities of sub-Saharan descent in Tripolitania, the western coastal region centered around Tripoli.

sources.citation: Ruth M. Stone, ed., The Garland Encyclopedia of World Music, vol. 1: Africa, Garland Publishing, 1998.

genres.name: Arab-Andalusian Nubah (Libya)
genres.start_label: Tradition arrived in Libya from Andalusia via North African migration after 1492; documented by Garland (1998) as part of the Maghrib classical tradition.
genres.note: Libyan maʾlūf belongs to the North African Andalusian tradition. Its nawba song cycles keep a melodic mode through successive sections with changing rhythmic patterns.

sources.citation: Ruth M. Stone, ed., The Garland Encyclopedia of World Music, vol. 1: Africa, Garland Publishing, 1998.

genres.name: Libyan sha'bi
genres.kind: popular music genre / urban folk hybrid
genres.start_label: Libyan sha'bi is documented as a popular urban folk music genre distinct from the classical Malouf tradition; an active tradition in 20th- and 21st-century Libya.
genres.note: Libyan sha'bi is a popular coastal song tradition centered in Tripoli, the northern capital, with the Tripolitanian style being the most widely recorded.

genres.name: Ashugh
genres.start_label: Armenian ashugh tradition documented from at least the 18th century, with Sayat-Nova (1712–1795) as the canonical key figure. The tradition predates his career and continues as a l
genres.note: Ashugh is an Armenian poet-singer tradition spanning the highland cities of Yerevan, Gyumri, and Vagharshapat, with historical roots across the entirety of historic Armenia.

genres.name: Kafeʾi
genres.kind: popular music genre / café performance tradition
genres.start_label: Entry describes kafeʾi as an Iranian popular café-music tradition active through much of the twentieth century.
genres.note: Kafeʾi was Persian popular music performed in Tehran's traditional neighborhood cafés and nightclubs. It developed from the work of moṭreb entertainers amid twentieth-century urban change.

sources.citation: Richard C. Jankowsky, vol. ed., Bloomsbury Encyclopedia of Popular Music of the World, vol. X: Genres: Middle East and North Africa, Bloomsbury Academic, 2015.

genres.name: Kūcheh-bāzāri
genres.kind: popular music genre / urban working-class song
genres.start_label: Entry describes kūcheh-bāzāri as particularly popular in the 1950s among traditional urban working-class Iranian audiences.
genres.note: Kūcheh-bāzāri is a Persian café-song style shaped by Arab popular music. Its singers used Persian lyrics while drawing on Arab melodies, rhythms, and vocal techniques.

sources.citation: Richard C. Jankowsky, vol. ed., Bloomsbury Encyclopedia of Popular Music of the World, vol. X: Genres: Middle East and North Africa, Bloomsbury Academic, 2015.

genres.name: Maḥalli
genres.kind: popular music genre / folk-derived popular form
genres.start_label: Entry describes maḥalli as drawing on sources mentioned in the Safavid period and active through the twentieth century.
genres.note: Maḥalli is Iranian popular song based on regional folk melodies or folk-inspired composition. Modern arrangements usually set short, simple tunes in verse-refrain form.

sources.citation: Richard C. Jankowsky, vol. ed., Bloomsbury Encyclopedia of Popular Music of the World, vol. X: Genres: Middle East and North Africa, Bloomsbury Academic, 2015.

genres.name: Moṭrebi
genres.kind: popular music genre / entertainer music tradition
genres.start_label: Entry describes moṭrebi as an Iranian popular entertainment music tradition.
genres.note: Moṭrebi names Persian popular entertainment associated with performers at weddings, cafés, and celebrations. Its practitioners could combine instrumental playing, song, dance, and acting.

sources.citation: Richard C. Jankowsky, vol. ed., Bloomsbury Encyclopedia of Popular Music of the World, vol. X: Genres: Middle East and North Africa, Bloomsbury Academic, 2015.

genres.name: Golha
genres.start_label: The Golha broadcast series ran from 1956 to 1979 on Iranian National Radio, producing over 1,400 episodes mixing classical Persian music with poetry under producer Davud Pirnia.
genres.note: Golha (Flowers) was a celebrated Persian music radio program broadcast nationally from 1956 to 1979, deliberately documenting classical and regional folk traditions across Iran.

genres.name: Zande/Azande musical traditions
genres.start_label: Azande musical traditions of South Sudan's southwest include likembe (thumb piano), kponingbo xylophone, and distinct dance forms, documented by ethnomusicologists.
genres.note: Azande music is the traditional music of the Zande people, who inhabit the far western region of South Sudan in Western Equatoria state.

genres.name: Palm-Wine Guitar
genres.start_label: In 1928, Kwame Asare was one of Ghana's first popular palm-wine guitarists; E. T. Mensah, the Ghanaian palm-wine guitarist, recorded for HMV; the Kru or dagomba style that most inf
genres.note: Palm-wine guitar is a coastal West African style shaped by Kru sailors' guitar music and important to early highlife in Ghana. Ghanaian guitarist Koo Nimo later performed the style internationally.

sources.citation: Ruth M. Stone (ed.), The Garland Handbook of African Music, 2nd ed., Routledge, 2008, pp. 105, 110-121.

genres.name: Anlo-Ewe Kinka
genres.start_label: Documented in fieldwork with Anlo-Ewe community; featured as audio examples on the Garland Handbook CD.
genres.note: Kinka is an Anlo-Ewe drumming and song tradition of southeastern Ghana. Both its drumming and singing are documented in recorded performance examples.

sources.citation: Ruth M. Stone (ed.), The Garland Handbook of African Music, 2nd ed., Routledge, 2008, p. 186.

genres.name: Agbekor
genres.start_label: Traditional war dance of the Anlo-Ewe of Ghana, listed alongside bawa of the Dagari and other Ghanaian traditional dances.
genres.note: Agbekor is an energetic Anlo-Ewe dance tradition of Ghana. Complex rhythms support the movement and distinguish its ensemble performance.

sources.citation: Ruth M. Stone (ed.), The Garland Handbook of African Music, 2nd ed., Routledge, 2008, p. 186.

genres.name: Fontomfrom
genres.start_label: Long-established Akan royal music; Ashanti women and men dance to the music of large cylindrical drums (fontomfrom); on installation an Asante chief performs the fontomfrom.
genres.note: Fontomfrom is Akan royal drum music used in chiefly ceremony. An Asante chief can perform it during installation to evoke predecessors.

sources.citation: Ruth M. Stone (ed.), The Garland Handbook of African Music, 2nd ed., Routledge, 2008, pp. 188-189.

genres.name: Ladino Song
genres.start_label: Entry surveys commercial Ladino recordings and a revival beginning in the 1960s; the 1992 fifth-centennial year was a watershed for recordings. Songs date back to the Iberian Jewis
genres.note: Ladino songs are Judeo-Spanish repertories carried by Sephardic communities. In Israel, concerts and recordings have helped revive and reinterpret songs once heard in homes, weddings, and festivals.

sources.citation: Richard C. Jankowsky, vol. ed., Bloomsbury Encyclopedia of Popular Music of the World, vol. X: Genres: Middle East and North Africa, Bloomsbury Academic, 2015.

genres.name: Musiqa Mizrahit
genres.start_label: Entry describes the genre's emergence and its incorporation of Greek laika, Yemenite and Moroccan religious songs, European ballads and Shirei eretz yisrael; its mainstream breakth
genres.note: Musiqa mizrahit is a broad field of Israeli popular music associated with Jewish communities from Middle Eastern and North African backgrounds. Its styles and production shifted toward mainstream pop from the 1980s onward.

sources.citation: Richard C. Jankowsky, vol. ed., Bloomsbury Encyclopedia of Popular Music of the World, vol. X: Genres: Middle East and North Africa, Bloomsbury Academic, 2015.

genres.name: Israeli rock
genres.start_label: Israeli rock began in the 1960s as local adaptations of Western rock and developed an original Hebrew-language character from the 1970s onward.
genres.note: Israeli rock developed from the 1960s in Tel Aviv and the coastal urban centers, blending Western rock with Hebrew lyrics and occasional Middle Eastern influences.

genres.name: Israeli psytrance
genres.kind: popular music genre / electronic dance music
genres.start_label: Israeli psytrance originated among Israeli travelers in Goa in the late 1980s–early 1990s and developed a major domestic production scene through the 1990s and 2000s.
genres.note: Israeli psychedelic trance emerged from the Tel Aviv coastal party scene in the early 1990s, becoming a globally influential dance music style.

genres.name: Klezmer revival (Israel)
genres.start_label: The klezmer revival began in the 1980s in Israel and the United States, reviving Ashkenazi Jewish folk music tradition after near-disappearance in the post-Holocaust period.
genres.note: The Israeli klezmer revival draws on Ashkenazi Jewish musical traditions, centered in Jerusalem and Tel Aviv through academic institutions and festival circuits.

genres.name: Dansi
genres.start_label: Documented by Garland (1998) as emerging from the 1940s in Kenya.
genres.note: Dansi names East African interethnic popular dance-band styles that flourished from the 1940s. Kenyan bands performed songs in multiple local languages and dialects.

sources.citation: Ruth M. Stone, ed., The Garland Encyclopedia of World Music, vol. 1: Africa, Garland Publishing, 1998.

genres.name: Beni Ngoma
genres.start_label: Associated by Garland (1998) with British marching bands of the Great War period; spread across East Africa from approximately 1914.
genres.note: Beni is an East African processional dance and music style modeled partly on British military bands. Performers imitated brass sounds on calabash kazoos and organized elaborate marching formations.

sources.citation: Ruth M. Stone, ed., The Garland Encyclopedia of World Music, vol. 1: Africa, Garland Publishing, 1998.

genres.name: Kolam
genres.start_label: Garland (2000) documents kolam as a living Sinhala masked theater tradition in southwestern Sri Lanka; references scholarly studies from 1966 onward. No origin date given.
genres.note: Kolam is Sinhala masked theater of southwestern Sri Lanka. Its performances combine a masked story, chorus, yak bera drum, and horanava reed instrument.

sources.citation: Alison Arnold, ed., The Garland Encyclopedia of World Music, vol. 5: South Asia: The Indian Subcontinent, Garland Publishing, 2000.

genres.name: Deshiya Gee
genres.start_label: Deshiya Gee (patriotic songs) emerged as a distinct Sri Lankan song tradition celebrating national identity, historical figures, and independence. The form developed particularly a
genres.note: Deshiya gee are Sinhalese folk songs found across Sri Lanka, associated with rural village life and agricultural cycles without concentration in one province.

genres.name: Sara griot tradition with kinde
genres.start_label: Traditional griot practice; no precise origin date established.
genres.note: Kinde is a musical arc-bow instrument of Sara griots from the southern Chad regions of Sarh and Moundou, used in praise-singing and ceremonial performance.

genres.name: Sara balaphone music
genres.start_label: Traditional Sara xylophone music; archive recordings documented from 1966.
genres.note: Sara balaphone music is a xylophone tradition from the Sara people of the Mandoul and Moyen-Chari regions of southern Chad.

genres.name: Kanembu flute and drum ensemble tradition
genres.start_label: Traditional Kanembu ensemble music; archive recordings documented 1960-80.
genres.note: Kanembu ceremonial flute and drum music comes from the Kanem region around Lake Chad in the north of the country, practiced by the Kanembu people.

genres.name: Chadian soukous influence
genres.start_label: Soukous influence on Chadian popular music developed post-independence from the 1960s.
genres.note: Soukous-influenced popular music developed in N'Djamena and the southern urban centers of Chad, drawing on Congolese rhythms mixed with local traditions.

genres.name: Chadian contemporary urban music
genres.start_label: Contemporary urban music scene in N'Djamena; approximate emergence from the 1990s-2000s.
genres.note: Contemporary urban music from N'Djamena, the capital of Chad in the southwestern region, fuses local traditional styles with Congolese soukous and global pop.

genres.name: Griot/Jeli kora tradition
genres.start_label: The griot/jeli tradition is of deep historical standing in West Africa; no single origin date is established for Senegal.
genres.note: The jeli griot kora tradition originates in the Mande heartland and is the dominant musical presence in the contemporary scene centered in Dakar in western Senegal.

sources.citation: Ruth M. Stone, ed., The Garland Encyclopedia of World Music, vol. 1: Africa, Garland Publishing, 1998, p. 422.

genres.name: Chimurenga
genres.start_label: Songs known as chimurenga 'songs of liberation' were based on mbira music and used to politicize rural people during Zimbabwe's independence war; Thomas Mapfumo developed chimureng
genres.note: Chimurenga is Zimbabwean electric-guitar music whose interlocking guitar and bass parts evoke Shona mbira patterns. Thomas Mapfumo is among its leading performers.

sources.citation: Ruth M. Stone (ed.), The Garland Handbook of African Music, 2nd ed., Routledge, 2008, pp. 5987, 8074-8087.

genres.name: Shona Mbira Music
genres.start_label: Mbira is described as a plucked lamellophone (also called sanza in southern Africa); Shona mbira song 'Tongore' recorded in 1972 in Zimbabwe; mbira music forms the structural basis
genres.note: Shona mbira music in Zimbabwe uses a plucked lamellophone in songs that include ancestral-spirit repertory. Recorded examples also show its connection to later chimurenga guitar playing.

sources.citation: Ruth M. Stone (ed.), The Garland Handbook of African Music, 2nd ed., Routledge, 2008, pp. 399, 488.

genres.name: Jit
genres.start_label: Jit emerged as guitar-driven township dance music in Zimbabwe from the 1950s onwards.
genres.note: Jit is a Zimbabwean popular music style that emerged in the 1960s from the Harare township scene, combining electric guitar with Shona musical rhythms.

genres.name: Tunisian Andalusian Music (Malouf)
genres.start_label: Tradition brought to Tunisia after the Reconquista (post-1492); documented by Garland (1998) as a living classical tradition.
genres.note: Tunisian maʾlūf is a local branch of North African Andalusian music. Its nubah suites combine sung poetry and instrumental sections through ordered melodic and rhythmic modes.

sources.citation: Ruth M. Stone, ed., The Garland Encyclopedia of World Music, vol. 1: Africa, Garland Publishing, 1998.

genres.name: Tunisian Gnawa
genres.start_label: Pre-colonial tradition documented by Garland (1998) as an active Tunisian practice.
genres.note: Tunisian Gnawa ceremony music accompanies possession and healing rites with singing, iron castanets, and the three-stringed gumbri lute. Annual rites honor the patron saint Sidi Marzuk.

sources.citation: Ruth M. Stone, ed., The Garland Encyclopedia of World Music, vol. 1: Africa, Garland Publishing, 1998.

genres.name: Fūndū
genres.start_label: Entry describes fūndū in the Tunisian musical context.
genres.note: Fūndū is a Tunisian vocal form that developed by the late nineteenth century. It combines maʾlūf performance style with melodic and rhythmic material from Tunisian popular traditions.

sources.citation: Richard C. Jankowsky, vol. ed., Bloomsbury Encyclopedia of Popular Music of the World, vol. X: Genres: Middle East and North Africa, Bloomsbury Academic, 2015.

genres.name: Mizwid
genres.start_label: Entry describes mizwid as a Tunisian popular genre.
genres.note: Mizwid is Tunisian urban popular music named for its double-reed bagpipe. Once strongly associated with migrant and minority communities in Tunis, it became a widely heard commercial style.

sources.citation: Richard C. Jankowsky, vol. ed., Bloomsbury Encyclopedia of Popular Music of the World, vol. X: Genres: Middle East and North Africa, Bloomsbury Academic, 2015.

genres.name: Ughniyya (Tunisian)
genres.start_label: Entry describes the Tunisian ughniyya as a distinct popular song genre.
genres.note: Tunisian ughniyya is a popular song form for solo voice, chorus, and instrumental ensemble, often alternating verse and refrain. It grew from urban maʾlūf contexts into twentieth-century broadcasting.

sources.citation: Richard C. Jankowsky, vol. ed., Bloomsbury Encyclopedia of Popular Music of the World, vol. X: Genres: Middle East and North Africa, Bloomsbury Academic, 2015.

genres.name: Zamrock
genres.start_label: Zamrock emerged around Zambia's 1964 independence and peaked in the 1970s. Key bands WITCH and Rikki Ililonga created a distinctly Zambian rock sound.
genres.note: Zamrock emerged in Zambia during the early 1970s, combining local musical influences with psychedelic rock, blues, and funk. Rikki Ililonga and Musi-O-Tunya were early figures in the scene.

genres.name: Kalindula
genres.start_label: Kalindula emerged as a distinct Zambian popular music genre in the mid-1980s, featuring electric bass and drawing on Bemba and Nyanja rhythms.
genres.note: Kalindula is Zambian popular music named for a bass instrument used in its ensembles. It combines local dance traditions with twentieth-century popular styles and homemade string and percussion instruments.

genres.name: Dansi
genres.start_label: Documented by Garland (1998) as emerging from the 1940s in Tanzania.
genres.note: Tanzanian dansi is urban dance-band music associated with Dar es Salaam. Bands attract followers through topical lyrics and a distinctive mtindo, or dance-and-fashion style.

sources.citation: Ruth M. Stone, ed., The Garland Encyclopedia of World Music, vol. 1: Africa, Garland Publishing, 1998.

genres.name: Beni / Mganda
genres.start_label: Documented by Garland (1998) as originating in the Great War period and spreading across East Africa; Tanzanian mganda form documented as continuing.
genres.note: In Tanzania, beni became known as mganda: a processional dance style with choreographed marching and calabash-kazoo imitations of military brass bands.

sources.citation: Ruth M. Stone, ed., The Garland Encyclopedia of World Music, vol. 1: Africa, Garland Publishing, 1998.

genres.name: C-pop
genres.start_label: Cheng states C-pop (Huayu liuxing gequ) first appeared in Hong Kong in the 1970s, replacing earlier regional terms for Mandarin pop.
genres.note: C-pop is an umbrella name for Chinese-language popular songs produced across regions and diaspora communities. The term appeared in Hong Kong in the 1970s.

sources.citation: Ya-Hui Cheng, The Evolution of Chinese Popular Music: Modernization and Globalization, 1927 to the Present, Routledge, 2023.

genres.name: Zhungdra
genres.kind: classical music of local Bhutanese origin
genres.start_label: Garland (2000) identifies zhungdra (gzhung-sgra) as one of three living Bhutanese music traditions; no origin date given.
genres.note: Zhungdra, or gzhung-sgra, is a Bhutanese music category described as locally originating, distinct from Tibetan-derived boedra and newer rigsar songs.

sources.citation: Alison Arnold, ed., The Garland Encyclopedia of World Music, vol. 5: South Asia: The Indian Subcontinent, Garland Publishing, 2000.

genres.name: Boedra
genres.start_label: Garland (2000) identifies boedra (Bodsgra) as one of three living Bhutanese music traditions of Tibetan origin; no origin date given.
genres.note: Boedra, or Bod-sgra, is Bhutanese music associated with Tibetan origins. It is distinguished locally from zhungdra and the modern rigsar style.

sources.citation: Alison Arnold, ed., The Garland Encyclopedia of World Music, vol. 5: South Asia: The Indian Subcontinent, Garland Publishing, 2000.

genres.name: Jhyaure
genres.start_label: Garland (2000) documents jhyaure as a living pan-ethnic Nepalese genre; no origin date given.
genres.note: Jhyaure is a popular Nepali dance-song form heard in the repertory of Gaine itinerant musicians and across several of the country's musical communities.

sources.citation: Alison Arnold, ed., The Garland Encyclopedia of World Music, vol. 5: South Asia: The Indian Subcontinent, Garland Publishing, 2000.

genres.name: Damai Baja
genres.start_label: Garland (2000) documents damai baja as a living hereditary tradition; Garland notes historical records of Damai instruments survive, and popular belief attributes origins to Middle
genres.note: Damai baja is an ensemble tradition of Nepal's hereditary Damai musicians. Its bands play for weddings, processions, and other life-cycle rites as both entertainment and auspicious ceremony.

sources.citation: Alison Arnold, ed., The Garland Encyclopedia of World Music, vol. 5: South Asia: The Indian Subcontinent, Garland Publishing, 2000.

genres.name: Adhunik Geet
genres.start_label: Adhunik Geet emerged as a Western-influenced modern song form in Nepal in the 1950s following the establishment of Radio Nepal. Paul D. Greene (2010) traces its development through
genres.note: Adhunik Geet are modern Nepali songs developed in Kathmandu from the 1940s, combining classical ragas with new literary texts and Western harmonic arrangements.

sources.citation: Paul D. Greene, 'Musical media and cosmopolitanisms in Nepal's popular music, 1950–2006,' Anthem Press 2010.

genres.name: Lok Geet
genres.start_label: Lok Geet is the generic Nepali term for traditional folk songs, covering regional oral traditions from the Hills, Terai, and Mountain zones of Nepal. It predates the modern period
genres.note: Lok Geet are Nepali folk songs spanning the hills, Terai plains, and mountain communities across the country, with no single province dominating the tradition.

genres.name: Ṣawt
genres.start_label: Ṣawt is dated to the mid-to-late nineteenth century and attributed in its modern form to Abdallah al-Faraj; documented into the early twenty-first century.
genres.note: Sawt is a Gulf musical genre practiced in Muscat and the northern coastal towns of Oman, combining melodic singing with frame drum rhythms.

genres.name: Razha / Al-Razfa
genres.start_label: Al-Razfa / Razha is a traditional Omani practice inscribed under UNESCO as part of the 2014 Al-Ayyala inscription shared with UAE.
genres.note: Al-Razfa is a communal performance in Oman and the United Arab Emirates. Two facing lines of men answer one another in sung chants while dancers move between them; verses often draw on Nabati poetry.

genres.name: Liwa
genres.start_label: Liwa is documented as a Bantu-Swahili diaspora tradition in coastal Oman, brought by communities of East African origin; active as a living practice.
genres.note: Liwa is a music and dance tradition of communities of East African descent along the Batinah coast and Muscat area in northern Oman.

genres.name: Luk Thung
genres.start_label: Garland (1998) documents luk thung as emerging after World War II, with early songs recorded in the 1950s–1960s; the genre is described as living and commercially active through th
genres.note: Luk thung is Thai popular music that took shape in the 1940s and speaks especially to rural and migrant working-class audiences. Its songs often evoke farm life, labor, and displacement.

sources.citation: Terry E. Miller and Sean Williams, eds., The Garland Encyclopedia of World Music, vol. 4: Southeast Asia, Garland Publishing, 1998.

genres.name: Li-ke
genres.start_label: Garland (1998) documents li-ke as a living Thai urban theater tradition; describes it as combining with luk thung after World War II. No precise origin date assigned.
genres.note: Li-ke is a Thai street-theater tradition performed on temporary urban stages. Its music and action mix older dance-drama repertory with popular songs familiar to contemporary audiences.

sources.citation: Terry E. Miller and Sean Williams, eds., The Garland Encyclopedia of World Music, vol. 4: Southeast Asia, Garland Publishing, 1998.

genres.name: Piphat
genres.start_label: Garland (1998) documents piphat as a continuing court/classical ensemble; references to French observer La Loubere in 1691 establish the ensemble's practice before the eighteenth c
genres.note: Piphat is a Thai classical ensemble combining winds and percussion. It serves courtly, ceremonial, and theatrical music, including ritual compositions.

sources.citation: Terry E. Miller and Sean Williams, eds., The Garland Encyclopedia of World Music, vol. 4: Southeast Asia, Garland Publishing, 1998.

genres.name: Stalile/Kuda
genres.start_label: Stalile is a communal group dance and Kuda another communal form within the Eritrean highland Tigrinya dance tradition.
genres.note: Stalile and Kuda are ceremonial music forms of Eritrea documented among highland and lowland communities; their precise regional distribution remains under research.

genres.name: Gaeda
genres.start_label: Gaeda is a communal Eritrean music form with a lead singer and drums, featuring socially conscious themes.
genres.note: Gaeda is a Tigrinya vocal tradition from the central highlands of Eritrea, performed during social gatherings and ceremonies in the Asmara region.

genres.name: MaHber Theatre Asmara music
genres.start_label: MaHber Theatre Asmara movement emerged in the late 1960s; piano bar culture documented from 2004+.
genres.note: The Mahber Theatre of Asmara is the principal venue of Eritrean performing arts, established in the highland capital city during the early twentieth century.

genres.name: Ṣawt
genres.start_label: Entry dates Gulf ṣawt to the mid-to-late nineteenth century and documents continued early-twenty-first-century performance.
genres.note: Ṣawt is an upper Gulf song tradition also performed in Qatar. Its characteristic ensemble pairs a singer playing the ʿūd with a mirwās drummer.

sources.citation: Richard C. Jankowsky, vol. ed., Bloomsbury Encyclopedia of Popular Music of the World, vol. X: Genres: Middle East and North Africa, Bloomsbury Academic, 2015.

genres.name: Nabaṭī
genres.start_label: Entry traces nabaṭī to a pre-Islamic age; its Gulf spread through migration is documented.
genres.note: Nabaṭī is vernacular Arabian poetry practiced in Qatar and across the Gulf. Its poems on love, praise, and tribal life are often recited or sung.

sources.citation: Richard C. Jankowsky, vol. ed., Bloomsbury Encyclopedia of Popular Music of the World, vol. X: Genres: Middle East and North Africa, Bloomsbury Academic, 2015.

genres.name: Küü
genres.start_label: Küü is the central instrumental form in Kyrgyz traditional music, performed on the komuz (three-string unfretted lute) or kyl-kyyak (bowed instrument). Pieces are programmatic, dep
genres.note: Küü is a Kyrgyz instrumental tradition associated with the northern Chui Valley around Bishkek, the cultural and political capital of Kyrgyzstan.
